extracted.intended_audience: educated general public and readers interested in political economy, social reform, and public policy
extracted.subtask_description: A magazine-style argumentative essay surveying the problems of private property (especially land), diagnosing social/economic harms, and discussing proposed remedies (limits on bequest, land nationalization, land-value taxation, diffusion of property, communal tenure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Property as incentive to industry
rubrics_metrics.description: Respect for the rights of property insures the chief stimulus to industry, intelligence, and thrift.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues that property rights create the spur to accumulation and productive effort; critiques of property must account for this incentive effect to avoid undermining industry and thrift.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of bequest (inheritance) as a social problem
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of bequeathing one's possessions has gradually increased and furnishes the most difficult part of the problem of property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large hereditary transfers (reinforced by entail and primogeniture) concentrate wealth and social position in a few families, remove healthy spur to work for heirs, and distribute 'subtle moral poison' through society. Remedies considered include placing limits on amounts bequeathable so large estates become divided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to primogeniture and entail
rubrics_metrics.description: Primogeniture and entail lead to concentration of estates, unwieldy management, and indifference to improvement; they are pronounced against by reformers and parliamentary commissioners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These customs yield excessively large estates that see waste, neglect of farming improvements, and social injustice; reformers favor diffusion of property and limitation of such legal devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diffusion of property vs. aggregation
rubrics_metrics.description: Diffusion of property rather than its aggregation is desirable; nationally property may accumulate more rapidly and comfort and content be more common when property is widely held.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mr. Kinnear's view cited: limits on bequests and favoring small parcels (as in French tenure) help social stability. But compulsory equal division at death (French system) is criticized as wrong; preference is for diffusion without destroying testatorial freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unearned increment (land value appreciation) is unjust
rubrics_metrics.description: The increase in land value conferred by population growth and community progress (the 'unearned increment') bestows wealth on owners without equivalent contribution and is an evident injustice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because community and public improvements largely create such increases, remedies (discussed later) should seek to capture or tax that increment rather than allow private windfalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Henry George's land-value taxation (single tax)
rubrics_metrics.description: Henry George proposes a tax on real estate equal to its rental as unimproved land (capturing the unimproved-site value), arguing that owners have no valid title except to improvements due to labor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under this plan owners keep value of buildings and improvements but lose unearned appreciation; George claims his tax would render other taxes unnecessary. Objections include moral attachment to private land ownership and fears that weakening tenure validity could encourage indiscriminate attacks on property in panic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nationalization of land (Spencer) and its limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposal to have government buy all land at market rates and let it on competition (nationalization) — intended to absorb future appreciation into the public revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism: enormous purchase cost (example: British lands valued very high), likely fiscal deficit (estimated annual deficit), enhancement of interest rates, abolition of a component of land value, and creation of objectionable government control and expense; practical feasibility and fiscal consequences must be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communal tenure as historical/alternative system
rubrics_metrics.description: Primitive communal cultivation (Russian mir, Swiss Allmend) guaranteed subsistence for every child born on the land and prevented wide disparity in fortune; supporters of communal systems cite stronger family feelings and social cohesion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communal tenure limited private accumulation and pauperism was less likely; the essay notes historical transition from communal to individual tenure and suggests communal systems inform reform debates, but does not fully endorse compulsory communal division.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main social difficulty: undue accumulation of wealth of any kind
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief social difficulty is undue accumulation of wealth of any kind (not only land): houses, mills, machinery, railways, and merchandise are limited and can concentrate to public detriment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments against excessive land-holding may generalize to other forms of wealth; policy should therefore address concentration across asset classes, not solely real estate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monopolies, cornering, and corporate concentration harm the public
rubrics_metrics.description: Merchants/speculators who corner commodities (coal, pork) or monopolizing companies (Standard Oil, Western Union) levy odious exactions, extort consumers, and harm the public interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monopolists often use legitimate business rules and corporate devices (sale, pledge of stocks) to avoid interference; legislation must be careful to prevent monopolistic concentration while not unduly stifling legitimate business. Examples and abuses are used as evidence of the problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property rules must adapt to demographic and industrial change
rubrics_metrics.description: Property rules devised with a limited glance into the future are strained by population growth, urbanization, manufacturing towns, and the drift to cities, producing awkward consequences not originally intended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historic legal forms fail to account for enormous increases in population and wealth; the resulting multiplicative increases in land value and landlord incomes create public deprivation and justify reconsideration of tenure rules and taxation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair taxation of landholders
rubrics_metrics.description: Landlords have grossly evaded their fair share of taxation over time (example: British land tax proportion greatly reduced), aggravating social inequity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluating property systems should include how burdens of taxation are distributed; remedial proposals may include shifting tax incidence to capture land value or limit tax privileges enjoyed by landed interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights of property depend on popular will and legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: In the last analysis the rights of property depend upon the popular will; a numerical majority can modify existing rights in what it deems the public good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because property rights rest on social sanction, widespread popular education, extension of suffrage, and organized labor increase political capacity to pursue reform; this political reality constrains the design and defense of property institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public provision and charitable institutions as palliatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Public parks, libraries, museums, galleries, hospitals, and public education have been established to reduce inequalities and serve the popular good; wealthy philanthropy also plays a role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These measures ameliorate some injustices of property but are described as partial/palliative rather than full solutions; the essay suggests expecting more structural justice may reduce the need for charity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Large estates are socially and economically unwieldy
rubrics_metrics.description: Very large estates become unwieldy in management, introduce intermediaries between landlord and tenant, and often lead to wasteful holding for sport rather than productive use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practical argument supports policies promoting smaller holdings and diffusion of property; family quarrels and entailed succession can harm land stewardship.
